newsitem.title: SPAIN: ETA killing of politician sparks clashes in Spain.
newsitem.headline: ETA killing of politician sparks clashes in Spain.

text.p: A young Spanish politician kidnapped and shot by ETA Basque guerrillas died on Sunday, sparking a violent backlash against the radical separatist group and international condemnation.
The Pope denounced the killing of the 29-year-old Basque town councillor Miguel Angel Blanco as an "act of blood". France called it "cowardly".
"After this murder, ETA is more isolated than ever," Basque political leaders said in a statement after an urgent meeting. "If they were not loved yesterday, they are despised today."

More than a million Spaniards vented their fury at the kidnapping in massive demonstrations across the country on Friday and Saturday. Officials said it was the most powerful display of national outrage at ETA in memory.

Almost all the gatherings were peaceful. But anger turned to violence on Sunday morning in the northern city of Pamplona, hours after hospital officials announced that Blanco had died of two gunshot wounds to the head.

Fierce clashes erupted between supporters and opponents of ETA who threw bottles and rocks at each other. Hundreds of Spanish youths shouting "Sons of Bitches" and "Murderers" attacked a handful of the rebel group's sympathisers.

Police in riot gear intervened, firing bullets and swinging batons at youths who tried to storm the headquarters of ETA's political wing, Herri Batasuna. Eighteen people were injured, state television said.
Police also stopped the youths from burning a bar where Herri Batasuna members meet in Pamplona.

When the clashes erupted in Pamplona, the city was packed with tens of thousands of visitors celebrating the world-famous bull-running festival which began one week ago. Most youths involved in the violence were dressed in the traditional fiesta white costume with red headbands and sashes.
The annual festival was suspended for one day to show "sadness and indignation" over Blanco's abduction and shooting. It was to resume Sunday night.
In Blanco's hometown of Ermua, thousands gathered in solidarity with his family on Sunday afternoon chanting "ETA, enough! We want peace!".

Basque leaders urged more demonstrations in the region's major cities on Sunday at 8 p.m. (1800 GMT). They proposed an hour-long work stoppage from noon on Monday in the Basque region to express "indignation" at the killing.
Spain's two leading trade unions called on workers across the country to stop at noon and observe 10 minutes of silence.
Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar was to attend Blanco's funeral in Ermua on Monday and then lead a mass demonstration in Madrid that evening.

ETA, which stands for Basque Homeland and Freedom, abducted Blanco on Thursday afternoon. The guerrillas killed him two days later after the government refused a demand to transfer about 500 ETA inmates scattered throughout the country to prisons in the autonomous Basque region by 4 p.m. on Saturday.
Blanco, a low-ranking member of Spain's ruling party, was found bound and bleeding on a roadside shortly after the deadline. He was taken to hospital in the Basque city San Sebastian in a coma.
Just before dawn on Sunday, doctors declared him "clinically brain dead".

The news of Blanco's death hit his family hard. "There was a very strong reaction, above all from the mother, sister and girlfriend," Doctor Garcia Urra said. The family had already endured an earlier mistaken announcement that he was dead.
Pope John Paul told followers: "I forcefully deplore this act of blood ... The killing of an innocent victim can never have justification."
Blanco's ordeal touched a raw nerve among Spaniards who in recent months have faced growing ETA violence. The group has killed nearly 800 people in a 29-year fight for independence.

Basque leaders and a government official in Madrid called for the isolation of ETA's political arm Herri Batasuna, a party which holds seats in the Basque and Navarre regional parliaments and the national congress.
Basque government head Jose Antonio Ardanza said Herri Batasuna members were "silent" accomplices to ETA and he vowed to stop cooperating with them in efforts to pacify the troubled region.
The Spanish government condemned the shooting on Saturday but made no further statements on Sunday following Blanco's death.
At several Spanish prisons, ETA inmates were reportedly separated from the main prison population to prevent them from being targeted for attacks.

Blanco was the 10th person killed by ETA so far this year. The group had kidnapped 77 people in its history and set deadlines to execute hostages only twice before. In both previous cases, the threat was carried out.
